analysis.one_liner: Makes some drug patents easier to invalidate so cheaper generic copies can reach the market sooner.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by Senator Murray with one Republican cosponsor, never received a committee vote and died when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: Brand-name drug companies list their patents in an FDA directory called the Orange Book, and those listings can block cheaper generic versions of a drug from being approved. This bill would require drug makers to file their patent information with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office within 30 days, publish it publicly, and invite anyone to challenge weak patents in a Patent Office review. A patent would only get fully listed — with all the blocking power that carries — if it survives that review or nobody challenges it in time.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients who buy prescription drugs, because easier challenges to weak patents mean more generic competition sooner, which typically lowers prices. Generic drug manufacturers also gain a clearer path to market.

how_it_helps.text: Drug makers must submit patent information to the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office within 30 days of a drug's approval (or of a patent's issuance), and the office must publish it and invite requests to challenge the patent's validity [S2][S3].

A patent would be only 'provisionally' listed in the Orange Book until the Patent Trial and Appeal Board confirms it is valid, or until the challenge window closes — 300 days after drug approval (or 15 months for patents issued later) [S3].
If a review cancels patent claims, the drug maker must ask to remove that patent information from the Orange Book list [S3].

Orange Book listings matter because a listed patent lets a brand-name maker trigger a hold on generic approval or sue a generic applicant to block its entry; stripping an invalid patent from the list removes that roadblock. (This is how the FDA's generic-approval system works; the bill amends it [S3].)

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers, whose later-issued patents would face a public challenge window and could be invalidated and removed from the Orange Book, weakening their ability to delay generic competition.

drawbacks.text: The bill only applies to patents issued after its enactment, so it would do nothing about the many patents already listed in the Orange Book or the patent thickets around existing drugs [S3].

It extends the window to petition for a patent review — overriding the normal one-year deadline and allowing 300 days from drug approval, or 15 months for later-issued patents — which adds litigation uncertainty around drug launches [S3].

An honest supporter would acknowledge the bill is narrow: it addresses one listing channel, not the broader set of tactics — settlements, pay-for-delay deals, citizen petitions — that also delay generics.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: A modest, low-cost transparency fix aimed at one specific tactic — keeping weak, late-filed patents out of the Orange Book — but its reach is limited to newly issued patents, so it would not dent the existing patent backlog that keeps many drug prices high.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP Committee, which never took it up, and it expired when the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on May 22, 2019, alongside Senator John Cornyn, making it bipartisan from the start [S1][S3][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the same day [S5].
No further action was ever taken — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — and the bill died at the end of the Congress on January 3, 2021 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers are better off, because they keep the ability to list newly issued patents in the Orange Book with no challenge window, preserving a tool that can delay generic competition and keep prices up.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led it in the Senate.

for.name: John Cornyn
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, its only cosponsor.

against.name: Lamar Alexander
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: His committee received the bill on referral but never scheduled a hearing or a vote on it.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — a Democrat and one Republican — but the bill never got a vote, so no record exists of how the full Senate would have split.

industries.note: Their newly issued patents would be published and opened to public challenge, and patents invalidated in review would come off the Orange Book — removing a tool used to block generic competitors and keep prices high. The industry's interest in this bill ran against patients seeking cheaper drugs.
Clearer, earlier paths to market when weak patents are invalidated, since fewer Orange Book listings would stand between them and FDA approval of cheaper copies.
A new stream of patent-validity challenges around drug approvals would create work, while some brand-side defense work shifts to the Patent Office process.
